title: Fatima al-Fihri Builds a Mosque in Fez
text:
In the early ninth century, a merchant named Muhammad al-Fihri left Kairouan, in what is now Tunisia, and settled with his family in Fez, a new city in Morocco then ruled by the Idrisid dynasty. He prospered. When he died, his two daughters, Fatima and Maryam, inherited his wealth.

According to the fourteenth century chronicle known as the Rawd al-Qirtas, the sisters decided to spend their inheritance on something lasting for their community. In 859 Fatima began building a mosque in the quarter where the families from Kairouan lived, and Maryam built another across the river, in the Andalusian quarter. The chronicle says Fatima bought the land, had the workers use clay and stone from the site itself, and fasted every day until the building was finished.

The Qarawiyyin mosque, named after the people of Kairouan, grew over the centuries into one of the great centers of learning in the Muslim world. Scholars came to teach law, theology, grammar, astronomy and medicine, and its library collected precious manuscripts. Later rulers enlarged the building many times.

Today the University of al-Qarawiyyin is often described as the oldest existing educational institution that still operates, though it became a modern state university only in the twentieth century.
lesson: An inheritance spent on the common good can outlast every private fortune. What a family builds for its community may be remembered for a thousand years.
people: Fatima al-Fihri, Maryam al-Fihri, Muhammad al-Fihri
source: Ibn Abi Zar, Rawd al-Qirtas (14th century)
caveat: The main source was written five centuries later, and the claim that it was the oldest university depends on how a university is defined.
